title: Masked Language Modeling (Encoder-Only)
oneLineScope: Encoder-only, bidirectional context: BERT and the masked-token objective that treats language understanding as a fill-in-the-blank problem.
prose:
Where we are. The autoregressive-lm node showed what you get when you keep only the decoder from the full transformer and train it to predict each token from its left context alone. That is exactly the right design for generation — you cannot condition on tokens you have not yet produced — but it is the wrong design for a different class of tasks. Named-entity recognition, coreference resolution, sentiment classification, extractive question answering: in all of these the input is complete and fixed, and the answer depends on context that may sit to the right of the position you are trying to understand. Conditioning only on the left half of the sentence is a structural handicap. This node describes the architecture that removes that constraint: the encoder-only transformer, trained with a masked language modeling objective.

The gist, in one paragraph. An encoder-only transformer is the encoder half of the full transformer, running alone: a stack of blocks with no causal mask, so every token position attends to every other position simultaneously. Because the attention is fully bidirectional, the representation at each position is informed by the entire sequence at once. The training objective must be redesigned to match: you cannot ask the model to predict the next token when it can already see it. Instead, BERT randomly blanks out roughly 15% of the tokens in each input and asks the model to predict what was there, using context from both directions. The model architecture is the same as the transformer encoder; the objective is a fill-in-the-blank task linguists call a cloze test. This is the BERT lineage.

Why it matters. BERT and the models that followed it established the pre-train-then-fine-tune paradigm for natural language understanding benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results across classification, sequence labeling, and reading comprehension tasks that had previously required specialized architectures. Understanding the masked LM objective — why the attention must be bidirectional, why a different training task is needed, what the 80/10/10 corruption mix does and why — is necessary for understanding both why BERT works and where the encoder-only family runs into its own structural limits.

Why bidirectional attention needs a different objective

The full transformer’s encoder uses self-attention with no causal mask: every position’s query can attend to every other position’s key. The \(n \times n\) score matrix is fully populated. That full bidirectional attention is the defining structural difference from the decoder-only model — and it immediately creates a training problem. If you tried to train this bidirectional architecture with a next-token language modeling objective, the model’s representation of token \(t\) would already have access to tokens \(t+1, t+2, \ldots\) Predicting \(x_t\) from the final-layer representation of position \(t\) would be trivial: the answer is already in the representation. You would not be modeling language; you would be copying. A different training objective is needed, one that creates a genuine prediction problem while retaining full bidirectionality.

The residual stream is still \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per token position, flowing through \(L\) identical encoder blocks each containing a full self-attention sublayer and a position-wise FFN, both wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. The output is a sequence of contextualized representations, one per token, each informed by the entire sequence simultaneously. What changes relative to the decoder-only model is entirely the training objective and the absence of the causal mask in attention.

The masked LM objective

Devlin et al. (2019) — BERT — solve the training problem with a cloze-style task. Before a training sequence is fed to the model, roughly 15% of its token positions are selected at random, and the model must predict the original token at those positions from context. This is the masked language modeling (MLM) objective. The loss is cross-entropy over the masked positions only:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid \tilde{x}_1, \ldots, \tilde{x}_n), \]

where \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of masked position indices and \(\tilde{x}\) is the corrupted sequence fed to the encoder. The unmasked positions contribute no direct loss term — their representations are updated only through backpropagation from the masked positions’ predictions, via the attention layers that connect them.

The task is harder than it looks. Unlike the next-token objective, where the model always has a definite correct history, the MLM objective forces the model to integrate information from both sides of a gap. The analogy to cloze tests in psycholinguistics and readability research is exact: the standard cloze test blanks out every fifth word and asks a reader to fill it in, scoring comprehension by accuracy. BERT’s version is stochastic and operates at the subword level, but the information-integration demand is the same.

The 80/10/10 corruption rule

The 80/10/10 corruption rule is a deliberate design choice, not an arbitrary hyperparameter. Of the 15% selected positions: 80% are replaced with a special [MASK] token; 10% are replaced with a randomly chosen vocabulary token; and 10% are left as the original token unchanged. The motivation is train–test mismatch.

At fine-tuning and inference time, the model sees real text — no [MASK] tokens appear in a sentiment classification input. If every masked position were replaced with [MASK] during pre-training, the model would learn to treat [MASK] as a special signal indicating “here is where you predict.” At inference, when there are no [MASK] tokens, the representations it learned to build for prediction would never activate in the same way. The 10% random substitution forces the model to maintain a skeptical, context-checking representation of every token position at all times: it can never be entirely sure any given token is genuine, so it must build representations that use surrounding context rather than relying on a literal read of each position. The 10% unchanged positions provide a small anchor signal. The arithmetic: only 1.5% of all tokens (10% of the 15% selected) are randomly replaced, so the language modeling signal is barely diluted.

Special tokens: [CLS] and [SEP]

BERT prepends a [CLS] token (for “classification”) to every input sequence. Because every position attends to every other, the final-layer representation of [CLS] accumulates information from the whole sequence. For sequence-level classification tasks — sentiment, textual entailment — this aggregate vector is used as the representation fed to the task-specific output head. A [SEP] token is appended at the end of each sentence segment, allowing the model to process sentence pairs — premise and hypothesis, question and passage — as a single packed sequence while retaining boundary information. This is the standard input format for tasks like natural language inference and reading comprehension.

Next-Sentence Prediction and the RoBERTa correction

BERT was pre-trained with a second auxiliary objective, next-sentence prediction (NSP): given two consecutive segments \(A\) and \(B\), predict from the [CLS] representation whether \(B\) genuinely followed \(A\) in the source corpus (positive) or is a randomly sampled segment (negative). The motivation was to provide discourse-level coherence signal for tasks like question answering and natural language inference, where the relationship between two sentences is central.

The honest account, disclosed by Liu et al. (2019) in RoBERTa, is that NSP appears to have been largely unhelpful. Models trained without NSP, on more data with larger batches, consistently outperformed BERT on downstream benchmarks. RoBERTa’s reanalysis suggested that the NSP task was too easy — sentence boundaries are strong cues that a simple model can exploit without learning deep discourse structure — and that BERT’s original training was significantly under-optimized relative to what the data and compute could support. NSP is documented here because it was an architectural component of the original BERT and because the RoBERTa correction exemplifies the kind of careful empirical revisionism the field needs: the original paper made a claim about a design choice, and a follow-up systematically falsified it.

BERT configurations

Devlin et al. released two model sizes. BERT-base: \(L = 12\) encoder layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\), \(h = 12\) attention heads, approximately 110 million parameters. BERT-large: \(L = 24\) encoder layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 1024\), \(h = 16\) attention heads, approximately 340 million parameters. Both were pre-trained on BooksCorpus (~800M words) and English Wikipedia (~2.5B words), using WordPiece subword tokenization with a 30,000-token vocabulary. Training BERT-large required 64 TPU v2 chips for four days — a scale that was exceptional in 2018, and one that RoBERTa (2019) already found was insufficient for the dataset size.

What encoder-only models do well, and what they cannot do

The bidirectional representations BERT produces are well-suited to tasks where the answer is a function of a complete, fixed input. Sentiment classification uses the [CLS] vector. Named-entity recognition uses the per-token vectors, one label per position. Extractive question answering identifies span boundaries from the per-token vectors. These are understanding tasks — mapping a fixed input to a label or a selected span — and the full-context representations carry the information needed.

What an encoder-only model cannot do is generate new sequences autoregressively. Because every position sees the full sequence, there is no well-defined next-token probability to decode from: extracting such a probability would require masking positions at inference time, which destroys the bidirectionality that is the architecture’s whole point. For generation tasks — summarization, translation, open-ended text production — you need either a decoder-only model or an encoder-decoder combination.

This structural boundary is the organizing question of the encoder-decoder-contrast node, which places encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder architectures side by side and maps out when each is the right choice. That node is the natural next step after reading both this one and autoregressive-lm.

diagrams.altText: A top-to-bottom stack. A sequence with a [CLS] token at the start, a [MASK] token mid-sequence, and a [SEP] token at the end feeds into an embedding plus positional encoding layer, then through L encoder blocks each with full bidirectional self-attention and an FFN. Bidirectional arrows between the [MASK] position and its neighbors emphasize full context. At the top, the [MASK] position's output feeds a linear projection and softmax to predict the original token. The [CLS] output is labeled as the aggregate representation used for classification tasks.

At the bottom: a sequence of token boxes reading '[CLS]', 'the', '[MASK]', 'sat', '[SEP]' from left to right, with [MASK] highlighted in red. Horizontal double-headed arrows among the tokens inside the self-attention box emphasize bidirectional context — every token connects to every other. Label all elements; structural diagram.

diagrams.caption: Bidirectional fill-in-the-blank versus left-to-right prediction: the contrast in context regimes between masked LM and autoregressive LM.
diagrams.altText: Two panels side by side. Left panel labeled 'Masked LM (encoder-only)': a sentence with one token blanked out, arrows coming from both left and right neighbors converging on the blank, with the label 'predict from full context'. Right panel labeled 'Autoregressive LM (decoder-only)': a sentence with each token predicted only from the tokens to its left, shown as a one-directional left-to-right arrow chain, with the label 'predict from left context only'.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual side-by-side illustration contrasting two context regimes. Left panel, labeled 'Masked LM (encoder-only)': a short sentence such as 'The [MASK] sat on the mat.' where [MASK] is highlighted. Arrows flow in from both the left tokens and the right tokens, converging on [MASK], labeled 'full bidirectional context'. A note below reads 'every position sees every other'. Right panel, labeled 'Autoregressive LM (decoder-only)': the same sentence without masking, but each token has an arrow arriving only from the left side — a left-to-right chain. The rightmost position shows 'predict next token', and a note below reads 'each position sees only its past'. Emphasize the directional difference between the two panels. No tensor shapes needed; this is the conceptual intuition diagram.

bibliography.citation: Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding." NAACL-HLT. arXiv:1810.04805.
bibliography.annotation: The defining BERT paper. §3.1 specifies the encoder-only architecture and the two pre-training objectives (MLM and NSP); §3.3 gives the 80/10/10 corruption rationale; Appendix A lists the BERT-base and BERT-large hyperparameters. The primary authority for all numbers cited in this node.

bibliography.citation: Liu, Y., Ott, M., Goyal, N., Du, J., Joshi, M., Chen, D., Levy, O., Lewis, M., Zettlemoyer, L., & Stoyanov, V. (2019). "RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach." arXiv:1907.11692.
bibliography.annotation: The systematic ablation study that found NSP largely unnecessary and BERT significantly undertrained. §4 ablates the NSP objective and larger batch / more data training. Essential for the honest account of what BERT actually showed versus what was claimed.

bibliography.citation: Alammar, J. "The Illustrated BERT, ELMo, and co."
bibliography.annotation: Clear visual walkthrough of the BERT architecture, the masked-token objective, the [CLS]/[SEP] tokens, and how the pre-trained model is adapted to downstream tasks. The best starting point for seeing the ideas before reading the paper.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J.H. Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), Chapter 11: "Fine-Tuning and Masked Language Models."
bibliography.annotation: A textbook treatment that situates BERT within the broader NLP landscape, covering pre-training objectives, fine-tuning, span-based and classification tasks. Useful for the reader who wants the full didactic context around the BERT family, not just the paper.
